title: Childhood in a Vice Grip
author: Brad Littlejohn
summary: Brad Littlejohn introduces his National Affairs essay on the digital vice industry by recounting how he went from a theologian and ethicist to the de facto ringleader of an amicus coalition in Free Speech Coalition v. Paxton, the case that upheld online age verification for pornography. He argues that the growing kids' online safety movement, for all its victories on bills like KOSA and the App Store Accountability Act, still lacks a single governing theory of the case. His proposed theory is that the problem is not fundamentally about speech but about markets: the internet functions as a vast marketplace dealing chiefly in addictive products, into which children are inducted while bypassing their parents. The excerpts reframe the policy debate away from how much we should limit children's rights of access and toward how much access to children we should grant for-profit companies, drawing an analogy to child labor in the Industrial Revolution. The closing move is a challenge to conservatives, who defend parental rights against the state but have given the ad man and the pornographer a free pass, and a call to guard the four walls of the home against intrusions by both state and market.
points: Littlejohn recasts kids' online safety as a question of contract and commerce rather than content, which sidesteps the First Amendment framing tech companies prefer.
He argues tech firms deliberately exploit the movement's scattered goals (mental health, parental rights, predators, privacy, age limits) to divide left and right.
The analogy he builds is that today's platforms employ minors as unpaid data miners, much as industrial firms once pulled children into mines and factories.
He faults conservatives for guarding the family against the bureaucrat while leaving the home open to advertisers and pornographers.
He warns that the coming fight over AI's access to children makes a clear economic theory of the problem more urgent than ever.
quotes: It was that the internet functioned as one vast marketplace, in which every user was treated as a commodity and was expected to commodify him- or herself, a marketplace that dealt chiefly in addictive products and into which children were inducted from an early age, bypassing their parents and thus dissolving the authority of the family.

Tech companies have sought to exploit this confusion and sow division in the ranks of this diverse movement, scaring off conservative lawmakers with fears of censorship and wooing progressives with talk of young people’s right to information.

But this is the wrong debate. Given that these for-profit companies are mostly in the business of purveying addictive products, the question we should be asking is, “just how much access to our children should we permit these companies to have?” The debate over kids’ online safety is, at root, a debate over the market’s access to childhood.

Just as companies tried to increase profits during the Industrial Revolution by pulling children out of their families and putting them to work in mines and factories, so today the largest companies on earth have discovered how to employ minors as unpaid data miners by enticing them with addictive products.

Imagine if the political debates of the late 20th century had focused on how much access drug dealers should have to school classrooms, whether door-to-door salesmen should be allowed to go from bedroom to bedroom within your home, or whether liquor stores should be able to open kiosks at playgrounds and soccer fields.
But if conservatives know intuitively that the bureaucrat should not come between them and their children, why have they granted a free pass to the ad man and the pornographer?

If the four walls of the home are the foundation upon which a free society rests, they must be guarded against uninvited intrusions by both the state and the market. Over the past generation, we have allowed these walls to dissolve under the fast-acting acid of the digital economy, mortgaging our civilization’s future in return for the convenience of free handheld babysitters.
In reality, these data miners wanted to open their minds for the same reason a fracking company wants to open up a rock formation: to get the profits flowing faster.
